title: Arun's Quiet Code
markdown:
In days long vanished — or last Civic Hall Saturday, which is much the same under sequins — Arun the rabbit adjusted the angle of a blinking LED with a paw that trembled just a smidge. His whiskers, usually focused calm, twitched like antennae picking up impending doom. Tonight was the annual Youth Showcase, and Arun was in charge of the main interactive display. He had crafted code so lean and elegant it practically hummed. The most beautiful things often work without fanfare. But he suspected the room was primed for something far more sparkly. Weeks of tinkering had left his burrow smelling of ozone and determination. Algorithms sang like a perfectly tuned fiddle. Optimization, he believed, was the unsung hero: invisible scaffolding under any dazzling facade.

“You’re fussing like a hen with a rogue feather, Arun,” chirped Tess the robin from a microphone stand. She cocked her head. “It’s just a showcase. Your code is magnificent. It’ll shine. Besides, the smell of stale biscuits is probably more exciting than your code to most of these folks.”

Arun sighed, disturbing lint on his tweed waistcoat. “Shine, perhaps. But will it be seen, Tess? Or will they all be mesmerized by Mr Silvertongue’s flourishes?”

The name sent a shiver down his spine. Head organizer, charisma as voluminous as his sequined jacket. Displays legendary: flashing lights, booming sound, more moving parts than a cuckoo-clock factory on a lively Saturday. Spectacle. Grand pronouncements. Expensive-sounding nonsense that made people nod even if it achieved nothing beyond making ears ring. Arun, who believed in quiet competence, found it exhausting. He had once overheard Silvertongue explain that a flashy display which promptly caught fire was simply “a fiery demonstration of artistic passion.”

The hall was a beehive. Teenagers milled, showcasing robotics that could tie shoelaces (eventually) and digital art that made you question the fabric of reality. Arun’s station, tucked near the refreshments to minimize pre-show anxiety, featured a simple screen: a serene, continuously evolving pattern, subtle as a well-placed pause in a witty sentence. People glanced, nodded politely, moved on, eyes already drawn to the promise of more noise. In the LED’s tiny glass, Arun saw his own ears twice — once as drawn, once as shimmer — and took the shimmer for confirmation that quiet might still be enough.

Then Mr Silvertongue took the stage, a whirlwind of shimmering fabric, voice resonating like a thousand unseen elephants. “Ladies and gentlemen, esteemed judges, and future titans of tomorrow! Prepare yourselves for a spectacle that will redefine engagement! A triumph of innovation! A marvel of marvels!”

The first boon arrived as gears: a colossal multi-tiered contraption of whirring metal, iridescent balloons that seemed to shimmer with captured moonlight, and projected dancing llamas. Ludicrously complex, a mechanical opera of questionable necessity. The audience gasped at unapologetic extravagance. Appreciative murmurs rippled — a stark contrast to the polite nods Arun’s display received. He felt like the quiet mouse in a room of roaring lions. He had considered adding blinking lights, just to belong, but his code would not allow such frivolous expenditure.

“See?” he whispered to Tess, who had fluttered to a table, eyeing a discarded crumpet. “They prefer the show. My little optimization feels like bringing a spoon to a fireworks fight.”

Tess pecked a crumb with surprising precision. “But your spoon is the one that can actually serve something. His fireworks just make noise and disappear. And frankly, that crumpet is more substantial than his entire contraption. Besides, that machine looks like it’s about to do something remarkably unfortunate.”

The second boon was balloons: one filled with what sounded like compressed glitter deflated with a mournful sigh, showering the front row with dull grey flecks. Dancing llamas flickered, their jig turning into a jerky shudder. A stern-faced badger judge scribbled furiously, far from impressed.

The third boon was silence, the inverse of what Silvertongue had wished: whirring gears ground to an alarming halt. Deafening quiet, heavier than any sound. The audience, moments before enthralled, shifted uncomfortably. Disappointment hung like an uninvited guest. Nervous coughs. Silvertongue, sequins garish under dimming spotlights, wrung his hands.

“My apologies! A minor technical recalibration. A feature, not a bug! A deliberate moment of reflective quietude!”

A teenager in the front row called out, “But what does it do?”

They had paid for wonder. They had received a grand expensive breakdown. Arun felt a knot tighten: he knew, with certainty, how to fix it. His code could streamline the system, make it responsive, fluid, reliable. But it meant stepping into the spotlight he dreaded, a rabbit walking toward a fox’s den of attention.

Tess nudged his paw with surprising force. “They’re looking for something, Arun. Not just flash, but real. Something that works. Something that makes them feel cared for.” She hopped onto his shoulder. “Your code isn’t just about being clever. It’s about making things nice for people. That’s important.”

Then, as granter enough for a damp civic evening, she offered a couplet like two pebbles into a looking-glass puddle by the door:

“What you hide in quiet code
will wear the wish the loudest showed.”

Arun took a deep shaky breath, polished wood and nervous teenagers in his lungs, and walked toward the stage, tweed feeling inadequate. At the microphone, the only sound was the faint defeated hum of the machine.

“Excuse me,” he began, barely a whisper, then steadier. “Mr Silvertongue’s display is very ambitious. It certainly grabs attention. But perhaps the issue isn’t just gears or balloons. It’s about how everything connects. How it responds.” He looked at expectant faces. “My code isn’t about the biggest splash. It’s about making sure every little bit works together, so the experience is smooth, warm, enjoyable. A friendly handshake rather than a loud shout.”

He explained without jargon: seamless transitions, efficient resources, a more responsive user experience. A well-crafted system, even if it seems plain, can create delightful shared moments, like perfectly brewed tea on a cold day. He was not boasting; he was sharing care and intention — technology serving people, not the other way around. A gentle breeze guiding a kite, not a hurricane ripping it apart. When a llama danced, lights pulsed in time, music swelled just so: a ripple of delight rather than cacophony.

A hush. They looked from the unassuming rabbit to the silent complex machine that had promised so much. Then thoughtful murmurs. They saw past glitter to the underlying mechanism: value not in deafening roar but in the gentle reliable hum of something that simply worked.

Mr Silvertongue, humbled and looking remarkably less sequined, looked at Arun. “I can explain everything except why it suddenly looks intentional,” he muttered, as the display flickered back to life, lights softer, movements more graceful. Arun’s quiet undercurrent had smoothed the chaos. Llamas danced with renewed vigour. The glitter balloon seemed to shimmer with genuine delight.

The audience clapped — not thunder for a spectacle that had narrowly avoided disaster, but a warm ovation for competence. They had come expecting dazzling performance and found something more valuable: the assurance that someone had cared enough to make it work without unnecessary drama.

Later, a sudden brief shower washed the world. Wet earth. New beginnings. A row of bicycles against the hall gleamed under streetlights, polished frames catching light like promises. In those wet wheels Arun saw his pattern again, twice, and this time the shimmer was not confirmation of hiding but of being usefully seen.

“You know,” Tess said, preening a damp feather, “sometimes the most expensive thing is a lie that’s beautifully packaged. The most valuable thing is a truth that’s been cared for. Like your code. Or a perfectly ripe berry.”

Arun’s whiskers relaxed. He had wished not to be the spectacle. What returned, inverse and kinder, was visibility of a different kind: a useful truth, shared with warmth, settling a room better than any fleeting firework. Streetlights shimmered on wet pavement — the shine that lasted after the sequins faded.
audience: young adults aged 16-18, teen anthology entry
